title: Why Does Alcohol Make You Feel Warm? The Science and the Risk
excerpt: Alcohol makes your skin feel warm while your core loses heat. Here's why the glow happens, why you feel cold later, why some people flush, and the hypothermia risk.
metaDescription: Why does alcohol make you feel warm? It widens skin blood vessels so heat escapes. Learn why you feel cold later, why you flush, and the hypothermia risk.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: why does alcohol make you warm
content:
**The short answer:** alcohol makes you *feel* warm because it widens the blood vessels in your skin. Warm blood from the middle of your body rushes outward, the nerve endings in your skin sense the extra heat, and you get that familiar glow. But the heat is moving the wrong way. Your skin warms up while your core loses heat faster, so your actual body temperature tends to drop. That's why the old idea of a nip of brandy to keep out the cold is a myth, and why drinking in cold weather is a real hypothermia risk.

This guide explains what's happening in your body when you get that warm feeling, why you might feel cold or sweaty later, why some people flush red, and when feeling hot or cold after drinking is a sign to get help.

> **When to see a doctor or get help.** Most warm, flushed feelings after a drink or two are harmless. **Call 911 if** someone who has been drinking is cold to the touch, pale or bluish (especially lips or fingertips), confused, very hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, vomiting while barely conscious, or has stopped shivering even though they're still cold. These can be signs of alcohol poisoning or hypothermia, and both are emergencies. **See a doctor soon if** you get hives, swelling of the lips or face, wheezing, or a pounding heart after small amounts of alcohol, or if you have frequent night sweats, fevers, or hot flashes that don't line up with drinking. This article is general information, not medical advice.

## Why Alcohol Makes You Feel Warm: The Blood Vessel Effect

Your body works hard to keep its core (your brain, heart, and other organs) at about 98.6°F (37°C). One of its main tools is controlling how much blood flows to your skin.

- **When you're cold,** the small blood vessels near your skin tighten (vasoconstriction). Less warm blood reaches the surface, so less heat escapes into the air. Your hands and feet get cold, but your core stays warm.
- **When you're hot,** those vessels relax and widen (vasodilation). More warm blood flows to the surface, where it can release heat. Your skin gets warm and pink, and you cool down.

Alcohol is a **vasodilator**. It relaxes the muscle in the walls of those small skin blood vessels, so they open up whether your body needs to cool down or not. Warm blood from your core floods into your skin. The temperature sensors in your skin, which sit right next to that blood, report "warm" to your brain. You feel cozy.

The key point is that your skin is not where your body temperature really matters. The warmth you feel is your core's heat moving outward to a place where it can escape. You're not making more heat. You're spending the heat you have faster.

### Why the glow shows up in your face first

The face, neck, ears, and upper chest have a dense network of small blood vessels close to the surface. That's why blushing happens there, and it's why alcohol's warming and reddening effect is most visible in the same places. Some people also notice warm hands and feet after a drink, which is the same thing happening at the body's extremities.

### Your brain plays a part too

Alcohol also acts on the brain, including the hypothalamus, the area that works like your internal thermostat. Research on alcohol and temperature control has shown that alcohol tends to lower the body's temperature set point and blunts the usual responses to cold. At the same time, the relaxed, pleasant mood from a drink makes you less bothered by discomfort in general. So you get warmer skin, a thermostat that's a little less alert, and a brain that cares less. All three point in the same direction: you feel warm and comfortable even if your body is cooling down.

## Does Alcohol Actually Keep You Warm?

No. This is one of the most persistent drinking myths, and it's the one that can actually hurt people.

Here's what alcohol does in the cold, step by step:

1. **It moves heat to your skin, where it's lost.** In cold air or wind, warm skin sheds heat much faster than cool skin. The vessel-widening that made you feel warm is now draining your core.
2. **It blunts shivering.** Shivering is your body's emergency heat generator. Rapid muscle contractions burn fuel and make heat. Alcohol dampens this response, so one of your best defenses against cold is weakened.
3. **It can lower your blood sugar.** Your liver normally releases sugar into your blood between meals. While it's busy processing alcohol, it's less able to do that. Low blood sugar leaves your muscles with less fuel for shivering, and it's more likely if you've been drinking without eating.
4. **It dulls the signals that you're getting cold.** Because your skin feels warm and your judgment is softened, you're less likely to zip up, go inside, or notice that you're shaking.

This is why public health agencies and outdoor safety groups consistently list alcohol as a risk factor for hypothermia, and why it shows up so often in cold-weather deaths. The classic picture of a rescue dog carrying a barrel of brandy to a stranded climber is charming, but medically it's backwards. Giving alcohol to someone who is already cold makes their situation worse.

### The "beer jacket" myth

"Beer jacket" is slang for that warm glow that convinces people they don't need a coat on the walk home. The feeling is real. The jacket isn't. You're losing heat faster than normal, you're less able to make more, and you're less likely to notice the danger. If it's cold enough that you'd normally want a coat, wear it, and wear it especially if you've been drinking.

### What about a hot toddy or mulled wine?

A warm drink does add a little heat to your body, and the warm liquid and steam feel soothing. If you're sitting by the fire after a day outside, a single hot toddy is unlikely to do any harm to a healthy adult. The problem is when people use alcohol *instead* of real warming, such as drinking to warm up while still outdoors, or before heading back out into the cold. The heat in the cup is small. The heat loss from the alcohol continues for hours. For actually warming up, a hot non-alcoholic drink, dry clothes, food, and shelter do far more. If you drink when you've got a cold, our guide on [whether alcohol helps a cold](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-help-a-cold) covers that question in detail.

## Why Do I Feel Hot After Drinking but Cold Later?

Many people notice a pattern: warm and flushed while drinking, then chilly, shivery, or clammy later that night or the next morning. That pattern makes sense once you know what alcohol is doing.

**While you're drinking,** blood is pushed toward your skin and you feel warm. At the same time, your body is quietly losing heat. You may also sweat a bit, which cools you further as it evaporates.

**As the alcohol wears off,** your blood vessels tighten back to normal. The warm skin feeling fades, and now you can feel the cooler core underneath. Your body may switch on shivering to catch up.

**During a hangover,** several things can make you feel cold or alternate between hot and cold:

- **Dehydration.** Alcohol makes your kidneys pass more water than usual, and less fluid in your body makes it harder to control temperature. Our guide on [whether alcohol really dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) explains how much this matters.
- **Low blood sugar.** Drinking without eating can leave your blood sugar low the next morning, which can bring on shakiness, sweating, and a cold, weak feeling.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol breaks up the second half of the night's sleep, and sleep loss on its own can leave you feeling cold and run-down.
- **A stress response.** As your body clears alcohol, it releases stress hormones that can cause sweating, a faster heartbeat, and a jittery feeling. This is mild for most people after a normal night out.
- **The inflammatory response.** Researchers think hangovers involve a short burst of inflammation, which may contribute to a general "coming down with something" feeling, including chills.

For most social drinkers, feeling a bit cold or sweaty after a big night is uncomfortable but not dangerous. If you regularly wake up drenched, see our guide to [night sweats after drinking](/never-hungover/night-sweats-after-drinking).

## Why Does Alcohol Make You Feel Hot (Not Just Warm)?

Sometimes the feeling goes past a pleasant glow into feeling genuinely hot, flushed, or sweaty. There are a few common reasons.

### More alcohol, faster

The vessel-widening effect is stronger the more alcohol is in your blood. Drinking quickly, drinking on an empty stomach, or switching to stronger drinks all raise your blood alcohol level faster, which can turn a gentle glow into a hot face and sweating.

### A warm room and a fast heart

Alcohol can raise your heart rate a little, and crowded bars, dancing, and heated rooms add to the effect. Your body responds by sweating and pushing even more blood to the skin. If your heart is pounding hard or skipping, see our guide on [a racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking).

### Histamine and other compounds in the drink

Some drinks, especially red wine and some aged or fermented drinks, contain histamine and related compounds. Alcohol can also cause your body to release histamine. In people who are sensitive, this can cause flushing, warmth, a stuffy nose, itching, or a headache. It's usually mild, but hives, swelling, or wheezing are signs of a true reaction and need medical attention.

### Hormones and hot flashes

For people in perimenopause or menopause, alcohol is a well-known trigger for hot flashes. The body's temperature control is already more sensitive during this time, and alcohol's effect on blood vessels can tip it over. Our article on [hot flashes after drinking](/never-hungover/hot-flashes-after-drinking) goes into this in more depth.

### Medications that react with alcohol

Some medicines cause a strong flushing reaction when combined with alcohol. The best-known is disulfiram (Antabuse), which is designed to do this. Others reported to cause flushing or a similar reaction in some people include metronidazole, some diabetes medicines, and certain other drugs. If a new medication suddenly makes you hot and flushed when you drink, ask your pharmacist.

## The Red Face: When Feeling Warm Comes With Flushing

A pink tinge after a drink or two is the normal vessel-widening effect. A fast, bright red flush, often with a hot face, a racing heart, and sometimes nausea after a single drink, is different.

That reaction is usually caused by **acetaldehyde**, the toxic chemical your body makes as the first step in breaking down alcohol. Normally an enzyme called ALDH2 clears acetaldehyde quickly. Many people, especially those of East Asian descent, carry a gene variant that makes this enzyme work poorly. Acetaldehyde builds up, widens blood vessels strongly, and causes the flush.

This matters for more than looks. Acetaldehyde is classified as a carcinogen, and research has linked the flushing response combined with regular drinking to a higher risk of esophageal cancer. Antacids that hide the redness, such as famotidine (Pepcid), don't remove the acetaldehyde. They just hide the warning sign. If this sounds like you, read our guide to [red face after drinking](/never-hungover/red-face-after-drinking) and our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive).

## Alcohol and Hypothermia: The Real Safety Issue

Hypothermia means your core temperature has dropped below about 95°F (35°C). It doesn't need arctic conditions. It can happen in cool, wet, or windy weather, and even indoors in an unheated space, especially when alcohol is involved.

### Situations where drinking raises the risk

- **Walking home in the cold** after a night out, particularly without a coat
- **Falling asleep outside,** in a car, or in an unheated room after drinking
- **Cold-water activities** such as boating, fishing, or swimming, where alcohol adds to the fast heat loss of cold water
- **Winter sports and camping,** including drinking around a campfire and then sleeping in a cold tent
- **Being outdoors at holiday events,** football games, or festivals in winter

### Warning signs of hypothermia

The early stages can look a lot like being drunk, which is part of what makes the combination dangerous.

- **Early:** shivering, cold and pale skin, numb hands, clumsiness, mild confusion
- **Worsening:** slurred speech, stumbling, drowsiness, poor decisions, weak pulse
- **Severe:** shivering stops even though the person is still cold, very slow breathing, unresponsiveness

Stopping shivering while still cold is a serious sign. It can mean the body's ability to make heat is failing.

### What to do

If you think someone has hypothermia, call 911. While you wait:

- Move them somewhere warm and out of the wind, handling them gently.
- Remove wet clothing and cover them with dry blankets, coats, or a sleeping bag, including the head and neck.
- Warm the center of the body (chest, neck, groin) first. Skin-to-skin contact under blankets can help.
- Give warm, sweet, non-alcoholic drinks only if they are fully awake and able to swallow.
- **Don't** give alcohol, don't rub their arms and legs hard, and don't put them in a hot bath.

### When alcohol alone drops body temperature

Very heavy drinking can lower body temperature even without much cold exposure. A low body temperature, with cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin, is one of the recognized signs of **alcohol poisoning**, alongside confusion, vomiting, seizures, slow or irregular breathing, and being hard to wake. If you see these signs, call 911. Don't leave the person to "sleep it off." Roll them onto their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and stay with them until help arrives.

## Who Is Most Affected?

Alcohol's warming illusion affects everyone, but some people are more at risk from it:

- **Older adults,** whose temperature control and sense of cold are often weaker to begin with
- **People with diabetes,** because alcohol can lower blood sugar and hide the signs of a low (see our guide on [alcohol and blood sugar](/never-hungover/alcohol-diabetes-blood-sugar-management-guide-2025))
- **People with a smaller body size or low body fat,** who lose heat faster
- **People taking sedating medicines,** such as sleep aids, some antihistamines, or anti-anxiety medicines, which can add to alcohol's effects on alertness and temperature control
- **Anyone drinking outdoors in cold or wet weather**

## Practical Tips: Enjoy the Glow Without the Risk

You don't need to give up a drink to enjoy a winter evening. A few habits keep the warm feeling from becoming a problem:

1. **Treat the warmth as a feeling, not a measurement.** If it's cold out, dress for the actual weather, not for how you feel after two drinks.
2. **Eat before and while you drink.** Food slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood and helps keep your blood sugar steady.
3. **Pace yourself.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, though this varies. Slower drinking means a gentler flush and less heat loss.
4. **Alternate with water.** It helps with hydration and slows your drinking.
5. **Plan the trip home.** Arrange a ride rather than walking a long way in the cold, and make sure friends get home and indoors.
6. **Never let a drunk friend sleep outside or in a cold car.** Get them somewhere warm and check on them.
7. **Notice unusual flushing.** If you go bright red after one drink, think about what that's telling you rather than hiding it.
8. **Warm up the right way.** After being outside, use dry clothes, a warm room, food, and hot non-alcoholic drinks.

## A Note on Recovery and DHM

The warm feeling while drinking and the cold, clammy feeling the next day are two ends of the same story: alcohol disrupting your body's normal balance. The most reliable ways to feel better the next day are still the basics. Drink less and slower, eat, hydrate, and sleep. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also take **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best seen as promising rather than proven. There is no good evidence that DHM changes how alcohol affects your body temperature or protects you from the cold, and it's no substitute for a coat and a safe ride home. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when.

## The Bottom Line

- Alcohol makes you feel warm by widening the blood vessels in your skin, which pulls warm blood from your core to the surface.
- That warmth is heat leaving your body. Your core temperature tends to fall, not rise.
- Alcohol also blunts shivering, can lower blood sugar, and dulls your sense of being cold, which is why it raises the risk of hypothermia.
- Feeling cold, shivery, or sweaty after drinking is common as the effect wears off and a hangover sets in.
- A fast, bright red flush after a small amount of alcohol can point to slow acetaldehyde breakdown and is worth paying attention to.
- Cold, pale or bluish skin, confusion, slow breathing, or not waking up after heavy drinking is an emergency. Call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does alcohol make you feel warm?**

Alcohol widens (dilates) the small blood vessels near the surface of your skin. Warm blood from your core flows outward, the temperature sensors in your skin pick up the extra heat, and your brain reads that as feeling warm. Your skin is warmer, but your body is actually losing heat faster, so your core temperature tends to drift down rather than up.

**Does alcohol actually keep you warm?**

No. It makes you feel warmer while making you lose heat faster. Widened skin blood vessels shed heat into the air, alcohol blunts shivering and the urge to put on more clothes, and it can lower blood sugar, which your body needs to make heat. In real cold, drinking raises the risk of hypothermia rather than protecting against it.

**Why do I feel hot after drinking but cold later?**

The warm feeling comes first, while blood is rushing to your skin. Over the next hours that same blood flow keeps leaking heat away, so your core temperature dips. As the alcohol wears off and your blood vessels tighten again, you notice the cooler core, which is why many people wake up chilly, shivery, or sweaty after a night of drinking.

**Why does my face get hot and red when I drink?**

Facial flushing is the same vessel-widening effect, and it's strongest in the face, neck, and chest. If you flush quickly and strongly after one drink, it can be a sign that your body breaks down acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of alcohol) slowly. That's common in people of East Asian descent and is linked to a higher risk of esophageal cancer with regular drinking, so it's worth taking seriously.

**Is the 'beer jacket' real?**

The feeling is real, but the protection isn't. A 'beer jacket' is the warm glow that makes people feel fine going out in the cold without a coat. Underneath, your body is losing heat faster than normal and you're less likely to notice when you get dangerously cold. Wear the coat.

**Can alcohol cause hypothermia?**

It can make it much more likely. Alcohol speeds heat loss, blunts shivering, dulls your judgment about the cold, and can lower blood sugar. Most cases involve cold exposure, such as falling asleep outdoors or walking home in freezing weather. Very heavy drinking can also lower body temperature on its own, which is one of the warning signs of alcohol poisoning.

**When should I see a doctor about feeling hot or cold after drinking?**

Call 911 if someone who has been drinking is cold to the touch, pale or bluish, confused, very hard to wake, breathing slowly, or has stopped shivering while still cold. See a doctor soon if you get hives, swelling, wheezing, or a racing heart after small amounts of alcohol, or if you have regular night sweats, fevers, or hot flashes that don't line up with drinking.
